extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim 'additional elements' amount to an 'inventive concept' (i.e., are 'significantly more' than a judicial exception) under the Alice/Mayo two-part test, per MPEP §2106.05(a) and related sections. Focuses on identifying additional elements, assessing conventionality, improvements to technology, specification support, and analyzing elements individually and in combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Additional elements amount to 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception? Examiners should identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception(s) and evaluate whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer by identifying additional elements and evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination with respect to the considerations the Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have identified (see MPEP §§ 2106.05(a)-(h)). This evaluation determines whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more (YES → eligible at Pathway C) or does not (NO → reject under 35 U.S.C. 101).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should first identify whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry over the identification of additional element(s) from Step 2A Prong Two. Use the full claim language and the specification to determine what additional elements are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether each additional element, alone or in ordered combination, contributes an inventive concept that is 'significantly more' than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that an inventive concept may arise from a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of conventional elements (e.g., BASCOM: installation of a filtering tool at a specific remote location with customizable features). Do not ignore combinations that together provide the inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry over Step 2A Prong Two conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should carry over their identification of additional elements and conclusions from Step 2A Prong Two into Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically carry over conclusions on considerations discussed in MPEP §§ 2106.05(a)-(c), (e), (f), and (h). Many of the considerations in Step 2B overlap with those already evaluated in Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-evaluate elements previously deemed 'insignificant extra-solution activity'
rubrics_metrics.description: If an element or combination of elements was previously considered insignificant extra-solution activity under MPEP § 2106.05(g), it should be re-evaluated in Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If re-evaluation finds the element is unconventional or otherwise more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, that finding may indicate the additional element is no longer insignificant and may contribute an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality: are additional elements well-understood, routine, conventional?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the additional elements are other than what is well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or simply append well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality to the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP § 2106.05(d) guidance. If additional elements merely append conventional computer or technological functions at a high level of generality, they likely do not supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze claim 'as a whole' and avoid oversimplifying
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the claim as an ordered combination, 'as a whole,' and avoid oversimplifying by looking too generally or ignoring specific claim requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not determine eligibility by treating elements in isolation if their combination provides the inventive concept. Be careful to account for the specific requirements of the claims (citing McRO and Diamond v. Diehr guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine each claim separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim should be examined for eligibility separately; claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dependent claim may be eligible if it recites additional elements that amount to significantly more even if the independent claim is ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to computer functionality or other technology (MPEP §2106.05(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field.' Improvement in computer functionality or technology is a key indicator of an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate improvement both in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Relevant Federal Circuit cases include Enfish, McRO, DDR Holdings, Amdocs, Visual Memory, etc. Look for a technical solution to a technological problem and specification disclosure showing how the improvement is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must provide technical explanation of asserted improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is asserted that the invention improves conventional functioning of a computer or technology, the specification should provide a technical explanation sufficient for one of ordinary skill in the art to recognize the claimed improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure must include sufficient detail; conclusory assertions of improvement are insufficient. The specification need not use explicit 'improvement' language, but the improvement must be apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art from the disclosure. Evidence submitted under 37 CFR 1.132 cannot be used to supplement the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must reflect the disclosed improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim itself must include the components or steps that provide the improvement described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims do not need to literally recite the phrase of improvement (e.g., 'thereby increasing the bandwidth'), but the full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation should be considered to determine if the claim reflects the improvement. Ensure the claim, as drafted, embodies the technical features that effect the improvement (citing Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method claims must be limited to computer implementation to show computer-functionality improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation must be limited to a computer implementation; if the scope can be performed mentally or verbally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics and RecogniCorp v. Nintendo: claims that can be performed mentally or without a computer are not improvements in computer technology. Ensure claim scope excludes purely mental/analog embodiments if relying on computer-functionality improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to non-computer technologies are equally relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in any technology or technical field (not only computer-related) may demonstrate patent eligibility if the claim achieves a new or improved technological way of performing a task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same improvement consideration across technologies (e.g., Rapid Litigation Management v. CellzDirect for life sciences). However, an improvement in an abstract idea itself (e.g., a better economic practice) is not an improvement in technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of features/circumstances courts have found may show an improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPEP lists example features that courts have indicated may show an improvement in computer functionality or technology (e.g., modifications to hyperlink protocol, inventive distribution of network functionality, specific data structures, unconventional network architectures, memory systems with programmable characteristics, technical details for image transmission, particular server structures, particular programming or UI implementations, security-profile methods, improved user interfaces, 3D spreadsheet navigation, license-restricted software operation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these case-based examples (Enfish; DDR; BASCOM; Research Corp.; Amdocs; Visual Memory; TLI; Apple/Ameranth; Finjan; Core Wireless; Data Engine; Ancora) to identify analogous facts where claims include concrete technical improvements rather than abstract ideas implemented on generic computers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of features/circumstances courts have found insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPEP also lists examples the courts have indicated may not be sufficient to show an improvement (e.g., functionally claimed menus, speed-up solely from general-purpose computer, mere automation of manual processes, recording/transmitting/archiving images with conventional tech, barcode affixation without technical detail, high-level instructions to display information, database usage improvements not improving functionality, arranging GUI info without technical means).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these non-examples (Ameranth; FairWarning; Credit Acceptance; TLI; Secured Mail; Interval Licensing; BSG Tech; Trading Technologies) to recognize when claimed features merely use conventional technology or are high-level business/organizational solutions rather than technical improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural outcome: Pathway C eligibility vs 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception itself (inventive concept found), the claim is eligible at Pathway C and the eligibility analysis is complete; if not, the claim is not patent-eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims found ineligible, examiners should follow MPEP § 2106.07 for forming an ineligibility rejection. Document the analysis of additional elements and the considerations relied upon.
